# <mark>CLINICAL PRESENTATION</mark>

<mark>A specific diagnosis in an individual or family with ichthyosis can help predict prognosis and is essential for genetic counseling.</mark> <mark>Several clinical features aid in distinguishing between different forms of ichthyosis, including:</mark>

- Age of onset  
- <mark>Presence of a collodion membrane at birth</mark>  
- <mark>Quality of scale (e.g., fine vs. coarse)</mark>  
- Presence or absence of erythroderma  
- <mark>Skin abnormalities in specific areas (e.g., palms, soles, ectropion, eclabium)</mark>  
- <mark>Adnexal involvement (e.g., alopecia, hair shaft abnormalities)</mark>  
- <mark>Extracutaneous manifestations or systemic involvement</mark>  

The appearance of the skin surface varies among types of ichthyosis. <mark>Visible scaling—ranging from fine to thick, plate-like flakes—may be present.</mark> Some patients exhibit thickened skin with or without obvious scaling. The term **hyperkeratosis** is used clinically to describe thickening of the stratum corneum, which may or may not be associated with visible scale.

<mark>A family pedigree can clarify the inheritance pattern.</mark> Parental consanguinity suggests autosomal recessive inheritance, although many autosomal dominant forms (e.g., **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis**) arise from spontaneous mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude this mode of inheritance.

Light microscopy is diagnostic in **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis**, showing characteristic cytoplasmic vacuolization and clumping of keratin filaments. Histopathology may also be helpful in select conditions such as **Refsum disease**, **neutral lipid storage disease**, and **acquired ichthyosis in sarcoidosis**. However, in many ichthyoses, histology lacks specificity. In such cases, genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis.

The development of ichthyosis in adulthood should prompt evaluation for underlying systemic disease, as it may be a cutaneous marker of malignancy, infection, or autoimmune disorders.

# ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

The stratum corneum, the terminal product of epidermal differentiation, functions as a protective barrier. It consists of corneocytes ("bricks") embedded in a lipid-rich extracellular matrix ("mortar"). Corneocytes are protein-dense, while the intercellular matrix is composed of hydrophobic lipid bilayers rich in ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids.

The structural integrity and hydration of the skin depend on the corneocytes, whereas the lipid matrix is primarily responsible for the permeability barrier that prevents transepidermal water loss. Normally, desquamation occurs in a controlled, invisible process where individual corneocytes detach and shed singly.

In ichthyosis, this balance is disrupted. There is abnormal scale formation—both in quality and quantity—compromised barrier function, and altered epidermal kinetics. Hyperkeratosis results from either increased production of corneocytes, delayed desquamation, or both.

Epidermal differentiation involves multiple coordinated steps, and defects at various stages can lead to similar clinical phenotypes. Known genetic defects include:

- **Mutations in *KRT1* or *KRT10***: Cause **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis**, characterized by abnormal keratin filament assembly and cytolysis in the suprabasal layers.
- **Mutations in *TGM1***: Encode transglutaminase 1, an enzyme critical for cross-linking the cornified envelope and attaching ceramides. Deficiency leads to **lamellar ichthyosis**, a severe form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI).
- **Deficiency of steroid sulfatase**: Results in **X-linked recessive ichthyosis**, where impaired hydrolysis of cholesterol sulfate disrupts corneocyte desquamation, leading to scale accumulation.

These molecular insights underscore the complexity of epidermal differentiation and highlight how disruptions in structural proteins, enzymes, or lipid metabolism can converge on a common clinical phenotype—ichthyosis.

# <mark>CONGENITAL ICHTHYOSIFORM ERYTHRODERMA</mark>

<mark>Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE) is apparent at birth, with affected newborns typically presenting with a taut, shiny **collodion membrane**.</mark> <mark>After the membrane sheds, the skin remains diffusely red and is covered with a fine, white, generalized scale (see Fig.</mark> 47-5). On the lower legs, the scale may become larger and darker. In contrast to lamellar ichthyosis, classic CIE usually lacks significant **ectropion**, **eclabium**, or **alopecia**.

Sweating capacity varies widely; many infants and children with CIE have **minimal sweating** and exhibit **severe heat intolerance**. Mucous membranes are generally spared. Palmoplantar involvement is variable—some patients show mild thickening, while others have normal palms and soles. Nails may develop **ridging**, but are often unaffected. As with all forms of ichthyosis, there is an increased risk of **dermatophyte infections** of the skin and nails.

Histopathologically, CIE is characterized by **hyperkeratosis**, **acanthosis**, and frequent **parakeratosis** (see Fig. 47-2C). <mark>Studies have demonstrated **markedly increased epidermal cell turnover**, which contrasts with the slower turnover seen in lamellar ichthyosis.[49]</mark>

Genetically, CIE is part of the autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) spectrum. A small subset of patients with CIE have mutations in the **$TGM1$** gene. Additionally, two siblings with a mixed phenotype—CIE and palmoplantar keratoderma—were found to have an autosomal dominant mutation in **loricrin**, a cornified envelope protein.[54] Genetic heterogeneity in ARCI is well established: **$TGM1$** has been excluded as the causative gene in some families with classic lamellar ichthyosis or CIE phenotypes, and mutations in other genes have been identified.

To date, mutations in **five additional genes** have been linked to nonsyndromic ARCI, and **two more** to syndromic forms. Two genetic loci—**12p11.2-q13** and **19p13.1-13.2**—are associated with ARCI, though the responsible genes remain unidentified (Table 47-3). A newly proposed **lipoxygenase pathway** may serve as a unifying mechanism linking many forms of ARCI.[20] However, this hypothesis requires further validation, and the connection between the most common ARCI mutation (**$TGM1$**) and lipid abnormalities remains unclear.

---

# EPIDERMOLYTIC HYPERKERATOSIS

In 1902, Brocq described **bullous ichthyotic erythroderma**, distinguishing the blistering form from nonblistering congenital ichthyotic erythroderma.[55] His report included three unrelated patients with variable clinical features, likely representing the first documented cases of what is now known as **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis** (OMIM #113800).

The condition is named for its hallmark histopathologic findings: **vacuolar degeneration** of the epidermis (epidermal lysis) and **hyperkeratosis**. It is also referred to as **bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma**, a descriptive term highlighting the neonatal onset of blistering, erythema, scaling, and erosions.

Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis follows an **autosomal dominant** inheritance pattern, with an estimated prevalence of **1 in 200,000 to 300,000** individuals. However, **spontaneous mutations** are common, accounting for up to **50% of cases**, which therefore lack a family history.

Clinically, the disease presents at birth with **widespread blistering**, **erythema**, and **skin peeling** (Fig. 47-6).

# <mark>ICHTHYOSIS</mark>

# <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>A heterogeneous group of skin diseases characterized by generalized scaling and, often, areas of thickened skin.</mark>  
Most types are inherited and usually present at birth; however, some forms are acquired.  
Scales may vary in size, color, and distribution across the body.  
May be accompanied by erythema, abnormalities of the skin adnexa, and other cutaneous findings.  
Can be associated with systemic manifestations such as failure to thrive, increased susceptibility to infection, atopic dermatitis, neurosensory deafness, and neurologic disorders.  
Histopathology is typically non-specific, except in conditions such as epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, neutral lipid storage disease, Refsum disease, and acquired ichthyosis associated with sarcoidosis.

---

## <mark>OVERVIEW</mark>

Early reports of ichthyosis in Indian and Chinese medical literature date back several hundred years B.C. The condition was later described by Robert Willan in 1808.

Ichthyosis may present at birth or develop later in life. It can be limited to the skin or occur in association with abnormalities in other organ systems. While several well-defined types of ichthyosis can be reliably diagnosed based on clinical and genetic features, the significant clinical heterogeneity and the influence of environmental factors on scaling can make specific diagnosis challenging in some patients and families.

Siemens introduced genetic concepts into the classification of ichthyoses, laying the foundation for modern understanding.

Advances in genetic research have identified the underlying gene defects in many forms of ichthyosis—classified as genodermatoses. A new classification system is emerging, based on molecular and genetic etiologies. Identifying the mutated gene provides insight into the pathophysiologic mechanism, enabling more rational approaches to diagnosis, classification, and treatment.

Grouping these disorders by inheritance pattern (Table 47-1) and by underlying molecular abnormality (Table 47-2) enhances understanding of their clinical phenotypes and disease mechanisms. However, further research is needed to fully elucidate how specific gene mutations and protein disruptions lead to clinical disease, and to develop targeted, innovative therapies.

# <mark>DISORDERS OF DNA REPAIR</mark>

# <mark>Xeroderma Pigmentosum</mark>

<mark>Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) serves as the prototype heritable disease with increased sensitivity to cellular injury.</mark> <mark>It is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by sun sensitivity, photophobia, early onset of freckling, and subsequent neoplastic changes on sun-exposed skin.</mark> <mark>Patients exhibit cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation and certain chemicals, due to defective DNA repair.</mark> <mark>Some individuals also develop progressive neurologic degeneration.</mark>

## Frequency

XP occurs with an estimated frequency of 1 in 1 million persons in the United States and 1 per 100,000 people in Japan. <mark>The disease is more common in regions where consanguineous marriages are prevalent, such as the Middle East.</mark> Cases have been reported worldwide across all racial groups, including whites, Asians, blacks, and Native Americans.

▲ FIGURE 140-2 Xeroderma pigmentosum.  
A. Pigmentary changes, atrophy, dryness, and cheilitis in a 16-year-old patient.  
B. Cheek of a 14-year-old patient with pigmented macules of varying size and intensity, actinic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma, and a surgical scar.  
C. Corneal clouding, prominent conjunctival blood vasculature, and loss of lashes.  
D. Myriads of pigmented macules of varying size and intensity and scattered achromic areas on the back, with marked sparing of sun-protected buttocks of a 14-year-old patient.

## <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

### Skin

Approximately half of XP patients experience acute sunburn reactions following minimal UV exposure, while the remainder tan normally without excessive burning. In all patients, numerous freckle-like hyperpigmented macules develop predominantly on sun-exposed skin (see Fig. 140-2). Non-melanoma skin cancer typically develops at a median age of 8 years in XP patients—a 50-year reduction compared to the general population—highlighting the critical role of DNA repair in protecting against skin cancer. Multiple primary cutaneous neoplasms, including melanomas, are common.

### Ocular Manifestations

Ocular abnormalities are nearly as prevalent as cutaneous findings and represent a key feature of XP (see Fig. 140-2C). The retina is shielded from UV radiation by anterior structures (eyelids, cornea, and conjunctiva), so clinical involvement is largely confined to these exposed areas. Photophobia is often an early symptom.

### Internal Malignancies

Review of global XP literature reveals an increased incidence of internal neoplasms. Oral cavity cancers—particularly squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue tip, a sun-exposed site—are frequently reported. Rare cases include brain tumors (e.g., sarcoma, medulloblastoma), spinal cord astrocytomas, and cancers of the lung, uterus, breast, pancreas, stomach, kidney, and testis, as well as leukemia. Overall, XP patients have an estimated 10- to 20-fold increased risk of developing internal malignancies.

## DISORDERS OF DNA REPAIR

### <mark>Xeroderma Pigmentosum</mark>

<mark>Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) serves as the prototype heritable disease with increased sensitivity to cellular injury.</mark> <mark>It is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sun sensitivity, photophobia, early onset of freckling, and a high incidence of skin cancers on sun-exposed areas.</mark> <mark>Patients exhibit cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation and certain DNA-damaging chemicals, due to defects in DNA repair.</mark>

Eight clinical phenotypes of DNA repair diseases have been recognized (e.g., XP, Cockayne syndrome, trichothiodystrophy). <mark>Mutations in 12 genes are associated with these phenotypes, with significant phenotypic overlap.</mark> <mark>Notably, mutations in a single gene can lead to multiple distinct clinical syndromes, and different genes can cause similar phenotypes.</mark>

<mark>For example, mutations in the **XPD (ERCC2)** gene are linked to:</mark>
- <mark>Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)</mark>
- <mark>XP with neurologic abnormalities</mark>
- <mark>XP-Cockayne syndrome complex</mark>
- <mark>Trichothiodystrophy (TTD)</mark>
- <mark>XP-trichothiodystrophy</mark>
- <mark>COFS syndrome (cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal syndrome)</mark>

<mark>The official gene names are listed in parentheses; complementation groups are denoted in uppercase (e.g., XPD).</mark>

### <mark>Nucleotide Excision Repair and Related Disorders</mark>

<mark>The **nucleotide excision repair (NER)** pathway repairs bulky DNA lesions, such as UV-induced photoproducts.</mark> <mark>NER is impaired in:</mark>
- <mark>**Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)**</mark>
- <mark>**Cockayne syndrome (CS)**</mark>
- <mark>**Trichothiodystrophy (TTD)**</mark>

<mark>Cells from patients with these disorders show increased sensitivity to UV light, with higher rates of cell death and mutation.</mark> <mark>However, only XP patients have a markedly increased risk of skin cancer.</mark> <mark>The reason for this differential cancer risk remains unclear.</mark>

<mark>Some proteins involved in these conditions have dual roles in **DNA repair** and **transcription**, particularly as components of the basal transcription factor **TFIIH**.</mark> <mark>For instance:</mark>
- <mark>**XPB (ERCC3)**: DNA helicase, unwinds DNA in the 3′ to 5′ direction</mark>
- <mark>**XPD (ERCC2)**: DNA helicase, unwinds DNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction</mark>

<mark>Mutations affecting different functional domains of these proteins may lead to distinct clinical phenotypes, contributing to overlap syndromes such as XP/CS or XP/TTD.</mark>

### XP Variant: Defect in DNA Damage Tolerance

<mark>The **XP variant** phenotype is clinically indistinguishable from classical XP but results from a defect in **translesional DNA synthesis**—a DNA damage tolerance mechanism—rather than NER.</mark> <mark>XP-variant cells cannot efficiently bypass DNA lesions during replication, leading to replication fork stalling and genomic instability.</mark>

### Mismatch Repair and Cancer Syndromes

The **DNA mismatch repair (MMR)** pathway is defective in:
- <mark>**Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC)**, also known as **Lynch syndrome**</mark>
- <mark>**Muir-Torre syndrome**, a variant of Lynch syndrome with cutaneous manifestations such as sebaceous adenomas and carcinomas</mark>

<mark>These conditions are associated with microsatellite instability and increased risk of colorectal, endometrial, and other cancers.</mark>

### <mark>DNA Helicases and Genomic Stability</mark>

**Helicases** are essential for DNA unwinding during replication, transcription, repair, and recombination. <mark>The **RecQ family** of DNA helicases is highly conserved from bacteria to humans.</mark> <mark>Three human RecQ helicases are linked to genetic disorders:</mark>
- <mark>**BLM** (mutated in **Bloom syndrome, BS**): chromosomal instability, cancer predisposition</mark>
- <mark>**WRN** (mutated in **Werner syndrome, WS**): premature aging, cancer risk</mark>
- <mark>**RECQL4** (mutated in **Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, RTS**): skeletal abnormalities, skin changes, cancer predisposition</mark>

<mark>All three are associated with chromosomal instability and increased cancer risk.</mark>

### BASC and Genome Surveillance

<mark>The **BASC (BRCA1-associated genome surveillance complex)** is a nuclear multi-enzyme complex centered on **BRCA1**.</mark> <mark>It includes key DNA damage response proteins such as:</mark>
- **ATM**
- **ATR**
- <mark>**MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) complex**</mark>
- <mark>**BRCA1**</mark>
- **BLM**
- <mark>**FANCD2**</mark>
- <mark>**MLH1**</mark>

<mark>These proteins physically interact to coordinate DNA damage detection, repair, and cell cycle control.</mark> Defects in any of these components can lead to genome instability and are associated with disorders including:
- **Ataxia telangiectasia**
- **Seckel syndrome**
- **Nijmegen breakage syndrome**
- **Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (BRCA1/2)**
- **Bloom syndrome (BS)**
- **Fanconi anemia (FA)**
- **Hereditary colon cancer**

Bloom syndrome and Fanconi anemia are discussed in detail in the following sections.

## <mark>DNA Repair Defects and Complementation Groups in Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP)</mark>

<mark>Most XP cells exhibit a normal response to x-ray treatment, highlighting the specificity of the DNA repair defect to ultraviolet (UV) radiation-induced damage.</mark> <mark>The defective genes responsible for the seven nucleotide excision repair (NER)-deficient forms of XP, as well as the XP variant, have been cloned, and their functions are under active investigation (see Chap.</mark> 109).

### <mark>Complementation Groups</mark>

<mark>Genetic heterogeneity among XP patients has been characterized through cell fusion experiments using cultured fibroblasts, which allowed the identification of distinct complementation groups (see Chap.</mark> 109). <mark>As of 2006, seven complementation groups—designated **XP-A** to **XP-G**—have been identified, each corresponding to a specific gene involved in NER (see Fig.</mark> 140-1). <mark>In addition to these groups, patients with clinical features of XP but intact NER are classified as **XP variants**.</mark> <mark>Cellular studies show these variant cells exhibit mild hypersensitivity to UV-induced inhibition of cell growth, an effect enhanced by caffeine.</mark> <mark>This defect is linked to mutations in **DNA polymerase eta (pol η)**, an error-prone polymerase responsible for translesion synthesis across UV-damaged DNA.</mark>

### Prenatal Diagnosis

Prenatal diagnosis of XP is feasible through two primary methods: measurement of UV-induced unscheduled DNA synthesis in cultured amniotic fluid cells, and molecular genetic testing of trophoblast cells obtained early in pregnancy.

### Drug and Chemical Hypersensitivity

Beyond UV radiation, XP cells show increased sensitivity to various DNA-damaging agents. These include:
- **Psoralens** and **chlorpromazine**
- **Chemotherapeutic agents** such as cisplatin and carmustine
- **Chemical carcinogens** like benzo[a]pyrene derivatives

The hypersensitivity likely arises because repair of the DNA damage induced by these agents involves pathways overlapping with the NER system, which is defective in XP.

## Treatment and Management

<mark>Management of XP focuses on early diagnosis, rigorous UV protection, and prompt detection and treatment of skin neoplasms.</mark> <mark>Diagnosis is based on clinical features and confirmed by laboratory tests demonstrating cellular hypersensitivity to UV radiation and defective DNA repair.</mark> <mark>Molecular genetic testing for causative mutations is increasingly transitioning from research settings to clinical diagnostics.</mark>

### Sun Protection

Patients must be educated to minimize UV exposure through comprehensive protective measures:
- Wearing **protective clothing**, **UV-absorbing sunglasses**, and **long hairstyles**
- Adopting lifestyle modifications to avoid sunlight
- Daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreens with a minimum **SPF of 15**

Regular skin surveillance is critical:
- Frequent self-examinations guided by trained family members
- Periodic full-body skin examinations by a physician (every 3–6 months, depending on disease severity)
- Documentation using **color photographs** of the entire skin surface, including close-ups of lesions with a ruler for size reference

### Treatment of Premalignant and Malignant Lesions

- **Actinic keratoses** (premalignant lesions) can be treated with:
  - Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen)
  - Topical **5-fluorouracil**
  - Topical **imiquimod**

- **Photodynamic therapy (PDT)** using topical 5-aminolevulinic acid followed by blue light exposure is effective for actinic keratoses in the general population. However, **no safety or efficacy data exist for XP patients**, and caution is advised due to the potential for abnormal cellular responses to light-based therapies.

- For extensive skin damage, **therapeutic dermatome shaving** or **dermabrasion** may be used to remove damaged epidermal layers. This promotes repopulation of the skin by relatively UV-protected cells from hair follicles and skin glands.

### Protection from Environmental Mutagens

Given the hypersensitivity of XP cells to chemical mutagens such as **benzo[a]pyrene** in cigarette smoke, patients should avoid exposure to tobacco and other environmental carcinogens. Clinical evidence supports this recommendation: one XP patient who smoked for over 10 years developed bronchogenic carcinoma at age 35, and another smoker developed lung cancer at age 48.

## Protect Your Skin: Key Recommendations

### Sun exposure can speed up skin ageing  
UV exposure is responsible for about 80% of visible signs of skin ageing, including wrinkles, fine lines, sagging skin, and age spots. Sun-protective habits and regular use of sunscreen can help preserve youthful, healthy skin.

### UV damage adds up over time and can be prevented  
Skin damage from UV radiation accumulates over a lifetime. <mark>UV rays from the sun can cause DNA mutations in skin cells, leading to sunburn, premature ageing, and an increased risk of skin cancer.</mark> <mark>Even without sunburn, skin damage can occur.</mark> Prevention is essential—and it’s never too late to start protecting your skin, regardless of skin type.

### Children are especially vulnerable  
Unprotected sun exposure during childhood and adolescence significantly increases the risk of skin cancer later in life. Encourage sun-safe habits early by using hats, protective clothing, and sunscreen on exposed skin when outdoors.

---

## How to Protect Your Skin?

The following recommendations summarize effective sun protection strategies.

### Avoid sunbathing  
The World Health Organization classifies ultraviolet (UV) radiation as a proven carcinogen. Sunbathing exposes large areas of skin to harmful UV rays. Using sunscreen during prolonged sun exposure does not fully protect against damage and may lead to longer sun exposure, increasing cancer risk.

### Avoid tanning  
There is no such thing as a "safe" or "healthy" tan. A tan is a sign that your skin is trying to protect itself from UV damage—it is an SOS response.

### Avoid tanning beds  
Tanning beds emit intense UV radiation and are proven to increase the risk of all types of skin cancer, especially when used at a young age. They also accelerate skin ageing.

### Protect skin when UV index is 3 or higher  
The UV index measures the strength of UV radiation, ranging from 0 (low) to 11+ (extreme). When the index reaches 3 or above, sun protection is necessary to prevent skin damage.

### Avoid the sun at midday  
UV radiation is strongest 2 hours before and after solar noon (when the sun is highest in the sky). Plan outdoor activities outside this window when possible. If you must be outdoors during peak UV times, use protective measures.

### Use shade and protective clothing  
Seek shade whenever possible, especially around midday. Wear:
- A wide-brimmed hat  
- Long-sleeved shirts and long pants  
- Sunglasses with UVA and UVB protection  
Tightly woven fabrics offer the best defense.

### Use sunscreen on uncovered skin  
When the UV index is 3 or higher, apply broad-spectrum sunscreen with:
- SPF 30 to 50+ (protects against UVB)  
- UVA protection (look for the UVA label)  
Apply sunscreen before going outside and reapply at least every 2 hours, or more often after swimming, sweating, or towel drying.

### Monitor your skin: Watch that SPOT!  
Check your skin regularly for:
- New growths  
- Changes in moles (size, shape, color)  
- Sores that don’t heal  
See a dermatologist or GP if you notice any of these signs. Early detection of skin cancer greatly improves treatment outcomes.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does consistent UV protection cause vitamin D deficiency?  
Sun-safe behavior as recommended does not typically cause vitamin D deficiency in individuals with fair skin who are active outdoors. Most people can maintain adequate vitamin D levels through incidental sun exposure and diet. If vitamin D levels are a concern, consult a healthcare provider about testing or supplementation.

# HEREDITARY DISORDERS OF GENOME INSTABILITY AND DNA REPAIR

## AT A GLANCE

- <mark>Genome instability characterizes a large group of inherited disorders with prominent cutaneous abnormalities; many have an increased cancer risk.</mark>  
- <mark>Genome instability is caused by impaired repair and/or maintenance of DNA.</mark>  
- <mark>**Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)** is a prototype disorder with impaired repair of environmentally induced DNA damage and a greatly increased frequency of sunlight-induced cancers.</mark>  
- <mark>Although these disorders are rare, heterozygote carriers of affected genes—potentially comprising several percent of the general population—may also have an increased risk of neoplasia.</mark>

---

## Overview

DNA serves as the carrier of genetic information and is constantly threatened by damaging agents such as oxidative stress, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, X-radiation, and chemical mutagens. <mark>While cells possess robust mechanisms to repair most DNA damage, failure to maintain genomic integrity can lead to abnormal cell function, cell death, or malignant transformation.</mark> If a damaged cell divides, its progeny may accumulate additional mutations, and progressive genomic instability can ultimately result in cancer.

The accumulation of multiple mutations in key genes within a single cell is required for malignant transformation. A **mutator phenotype**, characterized by increased mutation rates due to genome instability, is often considered a prerequisite for carcinogenesis. Without such instability, the probability of acquiring all necessary oncogenic mutations in one cell would be exceedingly low.

Genes implicated in hereditary genome instability syndromes can also contribute to sporadic cancers when somatically mutated, highlighting their critical role in suppressing tumorigenesis from an early stage.

Although these inherited disorders are rare (with incidences on the order of $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$), heterozygous carriers of pathogenic alleles may represent several percent of the general population. Most of these conditions follow autosomal recessive inheritance, so carriers are typically asymptomatic. However, epidemiological evidence suggests that carriers may still face a modestly increased risk of cancer.

---

## Patterns of Genome Instability

<mark>Genome instability manifests differently across syndromes:</mark>

- <mark>In **Bloom syndrome (BS)**, **ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T)**, and **Fanconi anemia (FA)**, spontaneous chromosomal breakage is observed in primary blood or skin cells, indicating intrinsic defects in DNA maintenance.</mark>
- <mark>In **xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)**, genome instability is primarily evident only after exposure to DNA-damaging agents such as UV radiation or chemical carcinogens like benzo[a]pyrene (found in cigarette smoke). Cells from XP patients show heightened sensitivity to UV-induced DNA damage due to defective nucleotide excision repair (NER).</mark>

<mark>The clinical severity in XP—particularly the high incidence of skin cancers and corneal scarring leading to blindness—results from the interaction between genetic susceptibility and environmental exposure.</mark> <mark>Notably, XP patients who rigorously avoid UV radiation can dramatically reduce or even prevent the development of skin cancer and ocular complications.</mark>

---

## DNA Repair Pathways and Disease Mechanisms

Several DNA repair pathways protect against specific types of damage:

- <mark>**Nucleotide excision repair (NER)**: Repairs bulky DNA adducts caused by UV light (e.g., cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers). Defective in XP.</mark>
- **Base excision repair (BER)**: Corrects small base lesions caused by oxidation or alkylation.
- **Double-strand break repair (via homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining)**: Impaired in A-T and FA.
- **Interstrand crosslink repair**: Defective in FA.
- **DNA damage response signaling**: Disrupted in A-T (ATM gene) and BS (BLM helicase).

Defects in these pathways lead to characteristic cellular phenotypes such as hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, increased mutagenesis, and chromosomal instability.

| **Fanconi anemia (FA)** | Hyperpigmentation, café-au-lait spots, hypopigmentation, skin atrophy | AML, head and neck SCC, gynecologic cancers | Congenital malformations, bone marrow failure | Autosomal recessive or X-linked | Increased chromosomal breakage with crosslinking agents | FANCA, FANCB, FANCC, ..., FANCP/SLX4 | Interstrand crosslink repair, homologous recombination |

> **Note:** BCC = basal cell carcinoma; SCC = squamous cell carcinoma; AML = acute myeloid leukemia.

---

## Clinical Relevance and Dermatologic Involvement

All of these disorders present with significant cutaneous manifestations, often prompting initial evaluation by dermatologists. Skin findings may include photosensitivity, pigmentary changes, atrophy, telangiectasia, and premature aging. Importantly, the skin serves as a visible indicator of systemic genomic instability.

Dermatologists play a key role in early diagnosis, cancer surveillance, patient education (especially regarding sun protection), and multidisciplinary management. Given the elevated cancer risk, regular screening and preventive strategies are essential.

Moreover, understanding the molecular basis of these rare syndromes provides critical insights into the broader mechanisms of DNA repair, aging, and cancer development in the general population.

# <mark>Quality of Life Measurement in Vitiligo: Position Statement of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology Task Force on Quality of Life and Patient Oriented Outcomes with External Experts</mark>

## <mark>Abstract</mark>

<mark>Members of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Task Force on Quality of Life (QoL) and Patient Oriented Outcomes, together with external vitiligo experts—including representatives from the EADV Vitiligo Task Force—reviewed available health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instruments for vitiligo and provided practical recommendations for assessing QoL in patients with vitiligo.</mark>

The **Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI)** was the most commonly used HRQoL instrument in vitiligo studies, enabling cross-country comparison of results. <mark>Several vitiligo-specific tools have been developed, among which the **Vitiligo Impact Scale (VIS)** stands out as an extensively validated instrument.</mark> <mark>The VIS-22 version includes established minimal important change values and clinical interpretation guidelines.</mark> However, it was developed in India, where specific cultural beliefs about vitiligo may influence responses.

<mark>The EADV Task Force recommends using the **DLQI** for adults and the **Children’s Dermatology Life Quality Index (CDLQI)** for pediatric patients as standard dermatology-specific instruments in vitiligo.</mark> <mark>There remains a critical need for a globally valid, cross-culturally adapted vitiligo-specific HRQoL instrument—either newly developed or improved from existing tools—with demonstrated responsiveness to change.</mark>

---

## Introduction

<mark>Vitiligo is the most common depigmenting skin disorder, affecting approximately **0.5% to 2%** of the global population across all age groups.</mark> <mark>It affects males and females equally, though women and girls tend to seek medical consultation more frequently.</mark> <mark>Management of vitiligo remains a significant challenge in dermatology.</mark>

<mark>Beyond its physical manifestations, vitiligo can lead to **severe psychological distress**, reduced quality of life (QoL), and increased risk of psychiatric comorbidities such as anxiety and depression.</mark> <mark>Patients with darker skin types often report greater HRQoL impairment due to more visible contrast in depigmentation.</mark> <mark>Cultural, social, and religious factors further shape perceptions of the condition, influencing stigma and coping mechanisms.</mark>

<mark>Psychoeducational interventions focusing on **acceptance and social adjustment** are often necessary.</mark> <mark>To accurately assess the burden of vitiligo, several disease-specific HRQoL instruments have been developed worldwide.</mark>

<mark>The EADV Task Force on QoL and Patient Oriented Outcomes has previously published guidance on selecting and using HRQoL instruments in dermatological conditions.</mark> <mark>Building on this work, the Task Force—alongside external vitiligo experts—conducted a review of HRQoL assessment tools specifically for vitiligo to provide evidence-based recommendations.</mark>

---

## Methods

The review involved members of the EADV Task Force on QoL and Patient Oriented Outcomes and external experts, including representatives from the EADV Vitiligo Task Force.

A literature search was conducted in **PubMed (1990–October 2021)** using the keyword combination: *"quality of life, vitiligo"*. This effort supported the development of a Position Statement and was not intended as a systematic review.

All volunteers were assigned sections of the identified publications for evaluation.

### Inclusion Criteria
- Publications written in English or with an English abstract

### Exclusion Criteria
- Review articles, guidelines, and study protocols  
- Studies without HRQoL assessment  
- HRQoL assessments in conditions other than vitiligo  
- Studies assessing HRQoL in multiple diseases without separate reporting or discussion of vitiligo data

Two co-authors independently assessed all publications. Discrepancies were discussed and resolved through consensus. The remaining studies were analyzed in detail to identify and evaluate HRQoL instruments used in vitiligo.

The Task Force endorses the use of the term **"quimp"** (quality of life impairment) in both clinical practice and research, and this terminology has been applied throughout the document.

# CHAPTER 72  
# Vitiligo  

Rebat M. Halder  
Sumayah J. Taliaferro  

## EPIDEMIOLOGY  

<mark>Vitiligo occurs worldwide, with a prevalence of 0.1 percent to 2.0 percent.</mark> <mark>In the United States, the estimated incidence is 1 percent.</mark> <mark>Vitiligo commonly begins in childhood or young adulthood, with peak onset between 10 and 30 years of age, although it may occur at any age.</mark> All races are affected, and both sexes are equally afflicted. <mark>A female preponderance has been reported, but this is likely due to increased reporting of cosmetic concerns among female patients.</mark>  

Familial clustering is common, though inheritance follows a non-Mendelian pattern. Approximately 20 percent of patients have at least one first-degree relative with vitiligo, and the relative risk for first-degree relatives is increased 7- to 10-fold.

## ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS  

Vitiligo is a multifactorial polygenic disorder with a complex pathogenesis. Although several theories have been proposed to explain the loss of epidermal melanocytes, the precise cause remains unknown. Significant progress has been made over the past two decades.  

Proposed mechanisms include:  
- Autoimmune  
- Cytotoxic  
- Biochemical  
- Oxidant-antioxidant imbalance  
- Neural  
- Viral  

These may contribute to the destruction of epidermal melanocytes. Genetic susceptibility also plays a significant role.

## Genetics of Vitiligo  

Vitiligo is characterized by incomplete penetrance, multiple susceptibility loci, and genetic heterogeneity. Inheritance likely involves genes related to:  
- Melanin biosynthesis  
- Response to oxidative stress  
- Regulation of autoimmunity  

The frequent association of vitiligo with autoimmune diseases has led to investigations of HLA associations. HLA types linked to vitiligo in multiple studies include **A2**, **DR4**, **DR7**, and **Cw6**.

## Autoimmune Hypothesis and Humoral Immune Response  

The association between vitiligo and autoimmune conditions is well established. Commonly associated disorders include:  
- **Thyroid disorders**: Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease  
- **Endocrinopathies**: Addison disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus  
- **Alopecia areata**  
- **Pernicious anemia**  
- **Systemic lupus erythematosus**  
- **Inflammatory bowel disease**  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**  
- **Psoriasis**  
- **Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome**  

The significance of some associations remains debated.

The most compelling evidence for an autoimmune basis is the presence of circulating autoantibodies in vitiligo patients. It remains unclear whether these antibodies are:  
- A consequence of melanocyte destruction (epiphenomenon)  
- Or active contributors to melanocyte damage  

Support for a pathogenic role comes from animal studies showing that pigment cell antibodies can appear before clinical depigmentation.

## Smyth Chicken Model  

The mutant **Smyth line chicken** is a well-established animal model for studying autoimmune vitiligo. This model has provided insights into aberrant immune processes involved in melanocyte destruction and the development of depigmentation.

## VITILIGO AT A GLANCE  

- Affects approximately **1 percent of the global population**  
- Chronic disorder with **multifactorial predisposition**  
- Triggering factors include trauma, sunburn, stress, and systemic illness  
- Characterized by **depigmented macules** that may slowly enlarge and new lesions may develop over time  
- Most common sites: **periorificial areas, face, genitals, mucous membranes, extensor surfaces, hands, and feet**  
- Associated with **autoimmune and endocrine diseases**, and rarely, **malignant melanoma**  
- **Fully developed lesions**: absence of melanocytes and inflammatory infiltrate  
- **Early lesions**: may show residual melanocytes and mild inflammation

## <mark>Premature Graying and Associated Findings in Vitiligo</mark>

<mark>Premature graying has been reported in vitiligo patients and their close relatives.</mark> <mark>Auditory and visual disturbances may occur in some individuals.</mark> <mark>Rarely, aseptic meningitis can result from the destruction of leptomeningeal melanocytes.</mark>

Vitiligo-like depigmentation is occasionally observed in patients with malignant melanoma. This is thought to arise from a T-cell-mediated immune response against melanoma cells that cross-reacts with normal melanocytes. A similar depigmentation phenomenon can occur during autologous T-cell-based immunotherapy for melanoma and may be associated with a more favorable prognosis. Depigmented areas around primary tumors may resemble halo nevi, but widespread, distant vitiligo-like lesions can also develop.

## <mark>Ocular Disease</mark>

<mark>Although most vitiligo patients do not report ophthalmologic symptoms, various ocular abnormalities may be present.</mark> <mark>Pigmentary changes in the iris and retina can occur.</mark> <mark>Choroidal abnormalities have been documented in up to 30% of patients, and iritis in approximately 5%.</mark> <mark>Uveitis is a common ocular manifestation.</mark> <mark>Exophthalmos may be seen in patients with coexisting Graves disease.</mark> <mark>Visual acuity is typically preserved.</mark>

## Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome

Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a rare systemic autoimmune disorder mediated by T cells, characterized by vitiligo, uveitis, aseptic meningitis, dysacusis, tinnitus, poliosis, and alopecia. <mark>It is associated with other autoimmune conditions such as autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, hypothyroidism, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and diabetes mellitus.</mark>

VKH syndrome classically progresses through three phases:

1. **Meningoencephalic phase**: Preceded by fever, malaise, nausea, and vomiting, patients may develop headache, meningismus, seizures, muscle weakness, or paralysis.
2. **Acute ophthalmic phase**: Patients present with photophobia, eye pain, and changes in visual acuity. Uveitis, iridocyclitis, choroiditis, and retinal detachment may occur, potentially leading to complications such as cataracts and glaucoma.
3. **Chronic or convalescent phase**: Vitiligo, alopecia, and poliosis typically appear during this stage, although they may occasionally precede ocular or neurological symptoms.

## <mark>Alezzandrini Syndrome</mark>

Alezzandrini syndrome is a rare condition characterized by unilateral facial vitiligo, poliosis, sensorineural deafness, and unilateral tapetoretinal degeneration. The etiology is not well understood, but autoimmune mechanisms—similar to those implicated in vitiligo and VKH syndrome—are suspected. Since its initial description in 1959 (in a patient with vitiligo, poliosis, and unilateral retinitis), only a few cases have been reported.

## <mark>Laboratory Tests</mark>

<mark>The diagnosis of vitiligo is primarily clinical.</mark> <mark>However, due to its association with other autoimmune diseases, screening laboratory tests are often useful.</mark> <mark>Recommended tests include:</mark>

- <mark>Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)</mark>
- <mark>Antinuclear antibody (ANA)</mark>
- <mark>Complete blood count (CBC)</mark>

<mark>Additional testing for antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies should be considered, especially if thyroid dysfunction is suspected.</mark> <mark>Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies are particularly sensitive and specific markers for autoimmune thyroid disease.</mark>

## <mark>Histology</mark>

<mark>Histopathologically, vitiligo is defined by the absence of melanocytes in lesional epidermis.</mark> <mark>At the margins of active lesions or in early lesions, a superficial dermal perivascular and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate may be observed, supporting a cell-mediated immune mechanism targeting melanocytes.</mark>

## <mark>Prognosis and Clinical Course</mark>

The prognosis and progression of vitiligo are unpredictable. The initial clinical subtype does not reliably predict the pattern of future skin involvement or disease activity.

## Treatment

Multiple treatment options are available for vitiligo (see Box 72-2). Most aim to restore skin pigmentation. Each therapeutic approach has distinct advantages and limitations, and no single treatment is suitable for all patients.

# Comparison of guidelines and consensus articles on the management of patients with acne with oral isotretinoin

## Abstract

<mark>Guidelines and consensus statements on the management of acne aim to provide evidence-based, expert-driven recommendations.</mark> <mark>This review compares current guidelines and consensus articles to compile recommendations on the use of oral isotretinoin in acne treatment.</mark> Ten common and clinically relevant questions are addressed, including indications for isotretinoin, recommended daily and cumulative doses, treatment duration, and laboratory monitoring. Special considerations such as timing of dermatologic procedures and potential associations with depression or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are also evaluated. A major limitation across guidelines is the use of differing acne classification systems. The recommended daily dose ranges from 0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg in European guidelines to up to 1 mg/kg in U.S. guidelines. Only European guidelines specify a minimum treatment duration of 6 months. All guidelines emphasize strict pregnancy prevention due to teratogenicity. Monitoring for symptoms of depression is recommended in European, French, and U.S. guidelines. Key clinical issues that remain inconsistently addressed include age indications, target cumulative dose, timing of procedures, isotretinoin-IBD association, acne flare prevention, and laboratory monitoring protocols. These topics require clearer inclusion in future guidelines, as they frequently arise in clinical practice.

## Introduction

Oral isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid), a natural metabolite of vitamin A, was approved for the treatment of acne vulgaris in 1982 by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and in 1983 by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Isotretinoin undergoes rapid intracellular conversion to all-trans retinoic acid and exhibits strong biological activity with low binding affinity for retinoid receptors. It effectively inhibits sebocyte proliferation, differentiation, and lipid synthesis both in vivo and in vitro, reduces *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*) colonization, and decreases inflammation and hyperkeratinization within the pilosebaceous unit.

The efficacy and safety of oral isotretinoin were evaluated in a systematic review by Vallerand et al., which included 11 randomized controlled trials published up to 2016. All studies demonstrated a clinically significant reduction in acne lesions with isotretinoin compared to control groups (placebo, systemic antibiotics, or other comparators). Adverse events occurred approximately twice as often with isotretinoin versus controls. Most were cutaneous and related to xerosis. Serious adverse events leading to discontinuation included Stevens-Johnson syndrome, severe cheilitis, photophobia, elevated liver enzymes, anorexia, headache, and depression.

This review compares current international and national guidelines and consensus statements on the use of oral isotretinoin for acne. Guidelines are intended to optimize patient care through evidence-based, critically appraised recommendations on treatment benefits and risks. Key areas of focus include indications for use, dosing strategies (daily and cumulative), treatment duration, laboratory monitoring, and special considerations such as procedural timing and potential psychiatric or gastrointestinal risks.

## Methods

Eligible publications included updated international and national guidelines and consensus articles containing recommendations on oral isotretinoin for acne. EMA recommendations were included as they inform drug prescribing frameworks in Europe. Guidelines published before 2012 or without a stated validity date were excluded. Only publications in English or French were considered.

Search terms included: *isotretinoin*, *systemic treatment*, *acne*, *guidelines*, *consensus*. Reference lists of included articles were manually screened for additional relevant guidelines or consensus documents. The final literature search was conducted on 20 May 2019.

## Myalgias and Musculoskeletal Concerns
Myalgias are the most common musculoskeletal complaint, occurring in 15 percent of patients. In severe cases, creatine phosphokinase levels should be evaluated to assess for possible rhabdomyolysis.

## <mark>Isotretinoin Therapy: Teratogenicity and Contraception</mark>
<mark>The greatest concern during isotretinoin therapy is the risk of administration during pregnancy, which can lead to severe teratogenic effects in the fetus.</mark> <mark>The drug is not mutagenic; its adverse effects occur during organogenesis.</mark> <mark>Therefore, isotretinoin should be reserved for patients who have not responded to other treatments.</mark>

<mark>Women of childbearing age must be fully informed of the risks associated with pregnancy while on isotretinoin.</mark> <mark>Patients must use two highly effective forms of contraception—such as an oral contraceptive combined with condoms and spermicidal jelly—starting at least one month before beginning therapy.</mark> <mark>Female patients must be thoroughly counseled and demonstrate understanding of contraceptive methods prior to treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>Dual contraception must continue throughout isotretinoin therapy and for one month after discontinuation.</mark>

<mark>In the United States, the FDA requires a strict risk management program known as iPledge.</mark> <mark>This computer-based system ensures adherence to pregnancy prevention protocols before, during, and after isotretinoin treatment.</mark>

## <mark>Dosing and Treatment Duration</mark>
<mark>The recommended daily dosage of isotretinoin is 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>A cumulative weight-based dosing target of 120 to 150 mg/kg over the course of therapy is often used, particularly in patients with variable dosing or interrupted treatment, as achieving this total dose improves the likelihood of long-term remission.</mark>

<mark>Patients with severe truncal acne—especially those with back and chest lesions, which respond less robustly than facial lesions—may require higher doses, up to 2 mg/kg/day.</mark> 

<mark>In patients with severe acne, particularly those with granulomatous lesions, disease flares are common at treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>To mitigate this, initial dosing should be low—often below 0.5 mg/kg/day.</mark> <mark>Pre-treatment with prednisone (40 to 60 mg/day) for 1 to 2 weeks may be necessary and sometimes continued for the first two weeks of isotretinoin therapy.</mark>

<mark>A typical course lasts 20 weeks, but duration is flexible.</mark> <mark>Therapy may be extended in patients who do not achieve adequate response.</mark> <mark>Additional improvement may occur for 1 to 2 months after stopping treatment, so complete clearance is not required before discontinuation.</mark>

## <mark>Laboratory Monitoring</mark>
<mark>Baseline laboratory tests should include a complete blood count and liver function tests.</mark> <mark>However, the most critical monitoring involves serum triglyceride levels.</mark>

- <mark>Baseline triglycerides should be measured before starting therapy.</mark>
- <mark>Repeat testing is recommended at 3 to 4 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.</mark>
- <mark>If levels are normal at 6 to 8 weeks and no risk factors are present, further testing may not be needed.</mark>
- <mark>If triglycerides exceed 500 mg/dL, monitoring should be frequent.</mark>
- <mark>Levels above 700–800 mg/dL warrant interruption of therapy or initiation of lipid-lowering treatment.</mark>
- <mark>Complications such as eruptive xanthomas or pancreatitis can occur at very high triglyceride levels.</mark>

## <mark>Diet and Acne</mark>
Several studies have suggested a potential role for diet in acne development. However, the overall evidence remains inconclusive. The impact of chocolate, sweets, milk, and fatty foods on acne requires further investigation. There is no strong evidence supporting routine elimination of these foods. Nevertheless, some patients report disease flares after consuming specific foods—particularly chocolate. Given these individual perceptions, it is reasonable to advise patients to avoid dietary items they believe trigger their acne.

## Acne Surgery
Acne surgery, involving the removal of comedones and superficial pustules, can accelerate the resolution of individual acne lesions. It was historically a mainstay of acne treatment.

# <mark>Clinical question 10: What are the recommendations for laboratory monitoring during treatment with isotretinoin?</mark>

<mark>The **European Medicines Agency (EMA)** recommends laboratory testing of **lipids and liver enzymes** before initiating isotretinoin treatment, and at **1 month and 3 months** after starting therapy.</mark> <mark>More frequent monitoring may be warranted in patients with underlying comorbidities.</mark>

<mark>The **European guidelines** align with the EMA, advising assessment of liver enzymes and lipid levels **before treatment**, at **1 month**, and then **every 3 months** thereafter.</mark> However, published guidelines generally lack detailed recommendations on laboratory monitoring beyond pregnancy testing.

<mark>The decision to perform laboratory monitoring should be individualized, based on the **treating physician’s clinical judgement**, taking into account the patient’s **risk factors, medical history**, and any **emerging symptoms**.</mark>

## Further evidence

A **systematic review and meta-analysis (2016)** evaluated studies on laboratory monitoring during isotretinoin treatment for acne, focusing on lipids, liver function tests, and complete blood counts. While isotretinoin was associated with **statistically significant changes** in mean values of white blood cells, liver enzymes, and lipid panels, these changes were not considered clinically high-risk. Only a **small proportion** of patients developed abnormal results. The authors concluded that **routine monthly laboratory testing is not justified** for all acne patients receiving standard-dose isotretinoin.

A **retrospective study of 515 patients** (574 treatment cycles) found:
- **Leucopenia** in 2.4% of cycles, none requiring treatment discontinuation
- **Non-clinically significant thrombocytopenia** in 1.6% of cycles
- **Elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT)** in 3.3% of cycles, without need for discontinuation
- **Lipid abnormalities** were more common
- **67.7% of all laboratory abnormalities** occurred within the first **60 days** of treatment

The study proposed a **risk-adapted monitoring strategy**:
- Assess **personal and family history** of lipid, liver, or hematologic disorders
- For **healthy patients**:
  - Perform baseline testing of **lipids and liver function**
  - Repeat testing at **month 2**, after reaching maximum daily dose
  - If results are normal, **further testing may not be necessary**
- If **abnormalities are present** or there is a **known lipid disorder**, continued monitoring is advised
- **Complete blood count (CBC)**: routine testing not recommended unless there is a known hematologic condition or risk factor

This study has been considered **practice-changing**, highlighting the issue of **overmonitoring** in isotretinoin-treated acne patients. Adopting this approach could reduce **unnecessary blood draws** and **healthcare costs**.

## Comments and conclusions

Clinical guidelines aim to optimize patient care based on the best available evidence regarding treatment **efficacy and safety**. However, limitations exist in both the evidence base and guideline quality.

As noted in the **US work group guidelines**, adherence does not guarantee successful outcomes. Guidelines should not be interpreted as establishing a **standard of care**, nor should they exclude other reasonable approaches. <mark>The final decision on therapy must be made collaboratively by the **physician and patient**, considering individual circumstances and disease variability.</mark>

The **European guidelines** emphasize that clinicians may be held **medically liable** if they deviate from recommended prescribing practices in the event of adverse outcomes.

A separate evaluation of acne guidelines published between **2013 and December 2016**, using the **AGREE II** tool and **Institute of Medicine** criteria for trustworthiness, found significant deficiencies in guideline quality. Improvements are needed to meet modern standards for guideline development.

Notably, there is **considerable variation** among current guidelines. A key step toward harmonization would be the adoption of a **common classification system for acne**.

# <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

<mark>Rubella is an enveloped RNA virus in the Togaviridae family.</mark> <mark>The virus is spread through direct or droplet contact from nasopharyngeal secretions.</mark> Infected individuals shed virus for 5 to 7 days before and up to 14 days after the onset of disease, with viremia unlikely after the rash appears. <mark>In most individuals, infection leads to lifelong immunity.</mark>

Congenital rubella occurs when a nonimmunized, susceptible pregnant woman is exposed to the virus. Transplacental infection of the fetus occurs during the viremic stage. The risk is greatest when fetal exposure happens in the first trimester. Congenitally infected infants may shed the virus through urine, blood, and nasopharyngeal secretions for up to 12 months after birth, making them a potential source of infection for other susceptible individuals.

# <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

## <mark>History</mark>

Primary rubella infection is typically a mild, subclinical disease, particularly in adults. <mark>The prodrome includes low-grade fever, myalgias, headache, conjunctivitis, rhinitis, cough, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.</mark> <mark>These symptoms may last up to 4 days and often resolve as the rash appears.</mark> Up to 50% of children with primary rubella infection may have a subclinical course or present with lymphadenopathy or rash alone (without prodrome). In contrast, older adults may experience more severe and prolonged prodromal symptoms, which can make clinical differentiation from rubeola (measles) difficult. <mark>The presence of Koplik spots in the oral mucosa favors rubeola.</mark>

As the prodrome resolves and the rash develops, some patients may exhibit an enanthem consisting of tiny red macules on the soft palate and uvula (Forschheimer spots). This finding is not diagnostic for rubella.

## Cutaneous Lesions

<mark>The exanthem appears 14 to 17 days after exposure and consists of pruritic pink to red macules and papules that begin on the face and rapidly spread to the neck, trunk, and extremities.</mark> Lesions on the trunk may coalesce, while those on the extremities tend to remain discrete. The rash typically lasts 2 to 3 days, in contrast to rubeola, which persists longer and clears starting from the head and neck. Desquamation may occur after the rash resolves.

## Related Physical Findings

Lymphadenopathy is most prominent in the posterior cervical, suboccipital, and postauricular lymph nodes and may be noted up to 7 days before rash onset. Node enlargement can persist for several weeks.

Arthritis occurs in up to 70% of infected adults, particularly women. Both small and large joints may be involved. Joint symptoms often begin as the rash fades and can last for several weeks. In some cases, symptoms may become persistent or recurrent, and joint swelling may progress to effusion.

# Laboratory Tests

A complete blood cell count typically shows leukopenia with relative neutropenia.

# <mark>ETIOLOGY</mark>

<mark>Most cases of erythema multiforme (EM) are related to infections.</mark> <mark>Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is definitively the most common cause, particularly in recurrent cases.</mark> The causal relationship between HSV and EM is well established through clinical experience, epidemiology, detection of HSV DNA in EM lesions, and the prevention of EM with antiviral suppression of HSV recurrences. <mark>A clinical link with herpes can be identified in approximately half of EM cases.</mark> <mark>Additionally, 10% to 40% of cases without apparent herpes symptoms are also found to be herpes-related, as HSV DNA is detectable in EM lesions by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.</mark> EM eruptions typically begin around 7 days after a herpes recurrence, although the interval can be shorter. Not every symptomatic HSV recurrence leads to EM, and EM can even follow asymptomatic HSV reactivation, making the connection easy to overlook by both patients and clinicians. HSV-1 is the primary subtype involved, though HSV-2 can also trigger EM; the relative frequency reflects general HSV subtype prevalence in the population.

<mark>*Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is the second major cause of EM and may be the leading cause in children.</mark> EM associated with *M. <mark>pneumoniae* often presents with atypical and more severe features compared to HSV-related cases.</mark> Establishing the link can be challenging, as clinical and radiological signs of pneumonia may be mild, and direct detection of *M. pneumoniae* is uncommon. PCR testing of throat swabs offers the highest sensitivity. Serologically, the diagnosis is supported by the presence of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies or a greater than twofold rise in immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies to *M. pneumoniae*. EM related to *M. pneumoniae* can recur.

Other infectious agents have been occasionally linked to EM in isolated cases or small series, but evidence for causality remains circumstantial. These include orf virus, varicella-zoster virus, parvovirus B19, hepatitis B and C viruses, and infectious mononucleosis, as well as various bacterial and viral infections. Immunizations have also been reported as potential triggers, particularly in children.

Drug-induced EM with mucous membrane involvement is rare. It remains uncertain whether such eruptions represent true EM or mimics such as annular urticaria or maculopapular drug eruptions with target-like lesions.

Idiopathic EM refers to cases where no HSV infection or other identifiable cause is found. These are relatively common in routine practice. However, HSV DNA has been detected by PCR in up to 40% of recurrent "idiopathic" cases. Some of these respond to prophylactic antiviral therapy, suggesting asymptomatic HSV reactivation as the trigger, while others do not, indicating possible alternative mechanisms.

EM-like dermatitis can also arise from contact sensitization. Despite clinical and histopathological similarities, these eruptions should be considered mimics of EM rather than true EM.

# PATHOGENESIS

The pathogenesis of EM has been most thoroughly studied in herpes-associated cases. It is unclear whether the same mechanisms apply to EM caused by other agents.

Infectious HSV has never been isolated from EM lesions. However, HSV DNA fragments—consistently including the viral polymerase (Pol) gene—have been detected in lesional keratinocytes using PCR. These fragments are localized primarily in basal and lower spinous layer keratinocytes, where the HSV Pol protein is also expressed. This leads to recruitment of HSV-specific T cells, including cytotoxic T cells. The initial virus-specific immune response is followed by a broader, non-specific inflammatory reaction mediated by autoreactive T cells.

# <mark>VIRAL DISEASES AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>Cutaneous lesions are an extremely common, and often the only, manifestation of many viral infections.</mark>  
Viruses can produce skin lesions either by direct replication in the epidermis, as is the case with papillomaviruses, poxviruses, and several herpesviruses, or as a secondary manifestation of replication elsewhere in the body.  
<mark>The direct effects of viral replication on epidermal cells and the inflammatory response of cell-mediated immunity combine to produce cutaneous lesions.</mark>  
Neoplastic transformation or viral latency followed by reactivation occurs with certain viruses.  
Laboratory diagnosis is by viral culture, microscopy, detection of viral nucleic acids or viral antigens, and/or serologic testing.  
Many effective antiviral drugs exist, and others are currently in development.  
Preventive techniques, most notably vaccines, have to date been the most effective means for controlling viral infection.

# Position statement: Recommendations on the diagnosis and treatment of Malassezia folliculitis

## Abstract

<mark>Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast that is part of the human mycobiome.</mark> <mark>Malassezia folliculitis (MF) occurs when the normally benign colonization of hair follicles by Malassezia yeasts becomes symptomatic, manifesting as pruritic papules and pustules.</mark> <mark>Although MF is commonly encountered in clinical practice, diagnostic and treatment approaches vary among dermatologists and across countries.</mark> Therefore, the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Mycology Task Force Malassezia folliculitis working group has developed these recommendations for the diagnosis and management of MF.

<mark>The recommendations include diagnostic methods, required positive findings before initiating therapy, and specific treatment algorithms for immunocompetent individuals, immunocompromised patients, and those with compromised liver function.</mark> In conclusion, this position statement provides a standardized clinical strategy for the diagnosis and management of Malassezia folliculitis.

## Introduction

Malassezia (formerly Pityrosporum) is a lipophilic yeast commonly found as part of the human mycobiome. <mark>Eighteen species have been identified, with *M.</mark> <mark>furfur*, *M.</mark> <mark>globosa*, *M.</mark> <mark>restricta*, *M.</mark> <mark>sympodialis*, and *M.</mark> <mark>pachydermatis* most frequently isolated from lesions of Malassezia folliculitis (MF).</mark> MF arises when the typically asymptomatic colonization of hair follicles by Malassezia becomes pathogenic, leading to pruritic papules and pustules, primarily in seborrheic areas. The condition is often associated with excoriations and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Common predisposing factors include excessive sweating, hot and humid climates, physical exercise, high sebum production, occlusion from sunscreens or emollients, recent use of antibiotics or corticosteroids, and immunosuppression.

Epidemiological data on the general prevalence of MF are limited. However, hospital-based studies report varying prevalence rates: 1%–2% in China, 3% in Saudi Arabia, 4% in Turkey, and 16% in the Philippines.

### Differential Diagnoses

- **Acne vulgaris**: Typically non-pruritic, affects the face and trunk, and is characterized by comedones along with papules and pustules (and sometimes nodules).
- **Acneiform eruptions**: Present with erythematous papules and pustules on the trunk, shoulders, and face; differentiation from MF often requires a punch biopsy.
- **Bacterial folliculitis**: Involves deeper follicular structures and may present with purulent discharge or systemic symptoms such as fever.
- **Eosinophilic folliculitis**: May be associated with elevated peripheral blood eosinophil counts and underlying conditions such as hematologic malignancies or HIV infection.

Given the frequency of MF in clinical dermatology, consistent diagnostic and therapeutic approaches are essential. However, current practices vary widely due to the availability of multiple diagnostic tools and treatment options. To address this variability, the EADV Mycology Task Force working group on MF developed this position statement based on expert consensus to standardize the diagnosis and management of MF.

## Materials and Methods

### The Expert Committee

The expert committee consisted of dermatologists from the EADV Mycology Task Force working group on Malassezia folliculitis, all with specialized expertise in mycology and MF. Conflict of interest disclosures were collected throughout the development of this statement.

### Aim and Target Audience

The primary aim was to establish evidence- and consensus-based recommendations for the diagnosis and management of MF. The target audience includes all healthcare professionals involved in the care of patients with MF. The recommendations are presented through diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms to facilitate clinical application.

### Literature Review

A systematic literature review was conducted to inform the recommendations. The full methodology and results of this review are provided in the supplementary information.

# MATERIALS AND METHODS

## The expert committee

The expert committee comprised dermatologists from the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Mycology Task Force working group on Malassezia folliculitis (MF), with specialized expertise in mycology and MF. Conflict of interest forms were collected throughout the development of this position statement.

## Aim of the position statement and target audience

The aim of this position statement is to provide evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and management of MF. The target audience includes all healthcare professionals involved in the care of patients with MF. The recommendations are presented through diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms.

## Literature review

A systematic literature review was conducted to inform the recommendations; detailed results are available in the supplementary information.

## Level of recommendation

The EADV Mycology Task Force working group on MF adopted a grading system (Grades A–D) used by the European Society for Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases to assess the strength of recommendations:

- **Grade A**: Strong support for a recommendation.
- **Grade B**: Moderate support for a recommendation.
- **Grade C**: Marginal support for a recommendation.
- **Grade D**: Support for a recommendation against use.

## Expert opinion

The expert panel consisted of 19 members of the EADV Mycology Task Force working group on MF. Consensus was achieved through an iterative process involving a written questionnaire followed by two video conferences. After the first video conference—during which questionnaire responses were reviewed and compared with findings from the systematic review—a draft summarizing discussions and proposed consensus points was circulated. The second video conference finalized the consensus on diagnostic and treatment recommendations.

## Consensus

Consensus was defined as agreement by at least 80% of the Task Force members.

# RESULTS

## Diagnosing Malassezia folliculitis

Diagnostic methods for MF are categorized as **recommended** or **supplementary**. Recommended methods are used to confirm or exclude clinical suspicion, while supplementary methods serve as adjuncts in cases with inconclusive results.

### Clinical presentation

MF typically presents as 2–4 mm pruritic papules and pustules on erythematous skin, predominantly in seborrheic areas such as the upper arms, chest, back, face, neck, and shoulders. Excoriations and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation may accompany lesions. Cysts have also been reported in some cases. The absence of comedones helps differentiate MF from acne vulgaris. Abscesses are not considered typical features of MF.

### Direct microscopic examination

Direct microscopy is performed using material from pustules, applied to a glass slide and dissolved in 10–20% potassium hydroxide (KOH). <mark>Diagnostic findings include unipolar budding yeasts (blastoconidia), conidia, and occasionally hyphae.</mark>

Staining techniques reported in the literature include:
- Parker blue
- Gram staining
- Methylene blue
- May-Grunwald-Giemsa (MGG)
- Chicago sky blue
- Calcofluor white/Blancophor (requires fluorescence microscopy)

Gram staining was evaluated in a study of 26 patients with MF, diagnosed based on at least two of the following criteria: (a) typical clinical presentation, (b) histopathological confirmation of Malassezia in inflamed hair follicles, or (c) clinical response to antifungal therapy. The method correctly identified MF in 22 of 26 patients, yielding a sensitivity of 84.6%. All six patients without MF were correctly ruled out, resulting in 100% specificity.

## <mark>Diagnostic Methods for Malassezia Folliculitis</mark>

<mark>Calcofluor white/Blancophor staining, which requires fluorescence microscopy, has been used for the detection of *Malassezia*.</mark> <mark>The diagnostic performance of Gram staining was evaluated in 26 patients with *Malassezia* folliculitis (MF), diagnosed based on at least two of the following criteria: (a) typical clinical presentation, (b) histopathological identification of *Malassezia* within inflamed hair follicles, or (c) clinical response to antifungal therapy.[20] Gram staining correctly identified 22 out of 26 patients, yielding a sensitivity of $84.6\%$.</mark> In the same study, all six patients without MF were correctly classified as negative, resulting in a specificity of $100\%$.[20]  

<mark>The diagnostic accuracy of potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation and May-Grünwald-Giemsa (MGG) staining was assessed in 49 patients with MF confirmed by cytological examination, fungal culture, and molecular analysis.[7] KOH correctly identified 40 patients (sensitivity $81.6\%$), while MGG detected all 49 cases (sensitivity $100\%$).</mark> <mark>Since all participants in this study had MF, specificity for KOH and MGG could not be determined.[7]</mark>

## Histopathological Examination

<mark>For histopathological evaluation, a punch biopsy is typically obtained from the central area of a follicular lesion and stained with haematoxylin-eosin (H&E) or periodic acid–Schiff (PAS).</mark> <mark>Characteristic findings include dilated and plugged hair follicles associated with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of eosinophils, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells.[6,21]</mark>

## <mark>Molecular-Based Detection</mark>

<mark>Molecular techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) can identify specific *Malassezia* species and genotypes, thereby supporting the diagnosis of MF.[6,19,22–24] However, because *Malassezia* is part of the normal cutaneous microbiota, molecular detection alone cannot confirm pathogenic involvement.[6,22] PCR methods used include real-time PCR, end-point PCR, restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP)-PCR, terminal RFLP (tRFLP), and PCR sequencing.[6,22] Despite their utility, neither PCR nor MALDI-TOF MS is routinely available in most clinical settings.</mark>

## Fungal Culture

<mark>Fungal cultures can be performed using specialized media such as Dixon’s agar, Leeming-Notman agar, or Ushijima’s medium.[19,25] Culture results may support the diagnosis of MF and provide antimycotic susceptibility data.</mark> However, contamination with non-pathogenic *Malassezia* from adjacent normal skin is a potential pitfall.[6,26] Additionally, growth rates vary among *Malassezia* species, which may skew results, and these culture methods are not widely accessible in routine clinical practice.[6,12]

## Wood’s Light Examination

<mark>During Wood’s light examination, ultraviolet light (320–400 nm) is applied to the skin, causing MF lesions to fluoresce with a green-yellow hue.</mark> In a study of 49 patients with MF confirmed by cytology, culture, and molecular methods, the sensitivity of Wood’s light was $65.3\%$. While this method can support clinical diagnosis, it lacks genus and species specificity (see Table 1).

## Comments on the Diagnosis of Malassezia Folliculitis

Direct microscopic examination (e.g., KOH, MGG) is a non-invasive method with high diagnostic accuracy and is recommended when clinical suspicion of MF exists. However, it is not currently required before initiating topical antifungal therapy. Although this may lead to diagnostic uncertainty, microscopic evaluation is not universally available, and delays in treatment initiation may occur. Topical antifungals have demonstrated cure rates up to $100\%$ in some studies, with minimal adverse effects (Table S5).[28,29] Therefore, in typical cases, the benefits of clinical diagnosis without mandatory microscopy outweigh the risks. Nevertheless, microscopic examination remains a valuable supplementary tool, particularly in refractory or atypical cases.

## Treatments for Malassezia Folliculitis

Evidence for MF treatment is limited to one randomized controlled trial evaluating oral itraconazole, along with several non-randomized comparative and non-comparative interventional studies, observational reports, and case series. Treatment recommendations are summarized in Table 2, with supporting evidence detailed in Tables S5 and S6.

# <mark>Pathology</mark>

<mark>In tinea versicolor, the organisms inhabit the stratum corneum.</mark> <mark>There is usually no dermal infiltrate.</mark> <mark>Yeast may be observed with hematoxylin and eosin staining alone, and PAS staining is confirmatory.</mark> <mark>Microscopic examination reveals clusters of oval budding yeast cells $3.5 \times 4.5 \mu \mathrm{m}$ in size, along with short, septate, and occasionally branching hyphae.</mark> <mark>This appearance is classically described as "spaghetti and meatballs" (Fig.</mark> 189-11). In *Pityrosporum* folliculitis, organisms are found in widened follicular ostia mixed with keratinous material. Rupture of the follicular wall can lead to a mixed inflammatory response and foreign-body giant cell reaction.

# <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

<mark>The clinical appearance of tinea versicolor is typically characteristic, and diagnosis is confirmed by KOH examination.</mark> <mark>Wood's lamp examination may reveal yellowish fluorescence of the affected skin.</mark>

# <mark>Treatment and Prognosis</mark>

## <mark>Tinea Versicolor</mark>

<mark>Multiple topical agents are effective for treating tinea versicolor.</mark> <mark>The most commonly used is 2.5% selenium sulfide shampoo, applied daily for 2 weeks, left on for at least 10 minutes, then rinsed off.</mark> <mark>Maintenance therapy with monthly application one to two times helps prevent recurrence.</mark> Topical azole antifungals are also effective. Ketoconazole 2% shampoo is lathered onto affected areas and left for 5 minutes, repeated for 3 consecutive days. Topical terbinafine 1% solution, applied twice daily for 7 days, has achieved cure rates exceeding 80%.

For extensive disease, frequent recurrences, or failure of topical therapy, systemic treatment is recommended. Oral ketoconazole (200 mg daily for 7 days) or oral itraconazole (200–400 mg daily for 3–7 days) is highly effective. A single 400 mg dose of itraconazole has shown over 75% efficacy and, in one study, was as effective as a 1-week course. Fluconazole is also effective, with a single 400 mg oral dose being sufficient.

## Pityrosporum Folliculitis

Pityrosporum folliculitis responds well to systemic antifungal therapy. Although controlled trials are limited, oral ketoconazole (200 mg daily for 4 weeks), fluconazole (150 mg weekly for 2–4 weeks), and itraconazole (200 mg daily for 2 weeks) are effective treatment options.
